d: Buttons allow players to prompt an action.
h:
GuiButtons are GuiObjects that allow players to perform an action. You can customize these buttons to provide context and feedback, such as changing the visual appearance or scripting audible feedback when a player interacts with a button.

There are two types of buttons which you can place on‑screen or in‑game:

  • A TextButton is a rectangle with text that triggers the Activated and/or SecondaryActivated event on click/tap.

  • An ImageButton is a rectangle with an image that triggers the Activated and/or SecondaryActivated event on click/tap. It features additional states for swapping the image on player hover or press.

Buttons on the screen

Buttons on the screen are useful to quickly guide players to various menus or pages. To add this type of button:

  1. In the Explorer window, hover over StarterGui, click the ⊕ button, and insert a ScreenGui.
  2. Hover over the new ScreenGui, click the ⊕ button, and insert either a TextButton or ImageButton.

Buttons on part faces

Buttons on a part are useful for allowing players to interact with parts. For example, you can let players step on a button to complete an action.

To add a button to the face of a part:

  1. In the Explorer window, hover over the part, click the ⊕ button, and insert a SurfaceGui.
  2. Hover over the new SurfaceGui, click the ⊕ button, and insert either a TextButton or ImageButton.

If you don't see the button, try choosing a different face (Top, Bottom, Front, Back, Left, or Right) for the Face property of the SurfaceGui.

Button appearance

Both TextButton and ImageButton inherit from GuiObject which contains properties like BackgroundColor3, Rotation, and Size. Buttons also accept the appearance modifiers common to most UI objects.

Unique to TextButton are various properties to change its visual appearance:

  • FontFace — The font used to render text.
  • Text — The text string rendered on the button.
  • TextSize — The line height of text in offsets.
  • TextColor3 — Color of the rendered text.

An ImageButton has several properties to change its visual appearance, including hover and pressed image variants to indicate a player's interaction with the button:

  • Image — The image that displays when a player is not interacting with the ImageButton.
  • HoverImage — The image that displays when a player is hovering their cursor over the ImageButton.
  • PressedImage — The image that displays when a player clicks/taps the ImageButton.

Script buttons

You can script an action when a player presses a button by connecting the button to the GuiButton.Activated event, or to GuiButton.SecondaryActivated for cross‑platform secondary input like right‑click on desktop and long press on mobile. For example, when you parent the following LocalScript to a button, the button changes to a random color every time a player clicks/taps it.

local button = script.Parent
local RNG = Random.new()

local function onButtonActivated()
    -- Randomize the button color
    button.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromHSV(RNG:NextNumber(), 1, 1)
end

button.Activated:Connect(onButtonActivated)

kid.simple: Buttons are UI pieces that players can click or tap to make something happen, like opening a shop or jumping into a round. A `TextButton` shows words, and an `ImageButton` shows a picture that can change when you hover or press it. You can put buttons on the screen or on the side of a part. A script listens for the `Activated` event to know when the button was pressed.
kid.analogy: A button is like a doorbell: it does nothing until someone presses it, and then it rings whatever you wired it to.
keyPoints: `TextButton` and `ImageButton` both fire the `Activated` event when clicked or tapped.
`SecondaryActivated` fires on right-click on a computer or a long press on a phone.
For on-screen buttons, add a `ScreenGui` to `StarterGui`, then add the button inside it.
For buttons on a part, add a `SurfaceGui` to the part, then add the button inside it; switch `Face` if you cannot see it.
`TextButton` uses `FontFace`, `Text`, `TextSize`, and `TextColor3` to change how its words look.
`ImageButton` has `Image`, `HoverImage`, and `PressedImage` so it can look different when hovered and pressed.
Buttons also have normal UI properties like `BackgroundColor3`, `Rotation`, and `Size`.

terms.event: A signal that something happened, like a button being clicked. You `:Connect` a function to run when it fires.
terms.Activated: The button's event for a normal click or tap.
terms.SecondaryActivated: The button's event for a right-click or long press.
terms.hover: When the mouse pointer rests on top of the button without clicking.
terms.cross-platform: Works on many kinds of devices, like computers, phones, and consoles.
terms.HSV: A way to describe color with hue (which color), saturation (how strong), and value (how bright), each from 0 to 1.

example.title: Change a button's color on every click
example.place: LocalScript inside a TextButton (inside a ScreenGui in StarterGui)
example.code:
local button = script.Parent
local rng = Random.new()

local function onButtonActivated()
	-- Pick a random hue from 0 to 1, with full color and brightness
	button.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromHSV(rng:NextNumber(), 1, 1)
end

button.Activated:Connect(onButtonActivated)
explain: `script.Parent` is the button, because the script sits inside it.
We make a random number maker with `Random.new()`.
Our function sets the button's background to a random bright color.
We connect the function to `Activated`, so it runs on every click or tap.

watchOut: Use `Activated`, not mouse-only events, so your button works on phones and consoles too.
Button scripts should be `LocalScript`s, since UI runs on the player's device.
If a button on a part will not respond, the `SurfaceGui` may need to be in `StarterGui` with its `Adornee` set to the part.
